claims.text: The local catalog and Pokemon TCG API model English Fossil as released on October 10, 1999.
The local catalog and Pokemon TCG API both model Fossil as a 62-card English Wizards of the Coast set.
Bulbapedia describes Fossil as an English expansion corresponding to the Japanese Mystery of the Fossils era, while the local catalog treats the English release as its own release_family_id.

The local Fossil catalog's opening holo rows include Aerodactyl, Articuno, Dragonite, Gengar, Lapras, Moltres, and Zapdos, while Mysterious Fossil appears as the common trainer row that makes the fossil mechanic legible.
The local Fossil artist credits for the promoted rows include Kagemaru Himeno, Mitsuhiro Arita, Keiji Kinebuchi, and Ken Sugimori.

Fossil matters because it turns the early binder into an excavation site: prehistoric Pokemon, legendary birds, ghost-line atmosphere, and the Mysterious Fossil trainer make discovery itself part of the card-game apparatus.

narrative.why_it_matters: Fossil is one of those early sets that changes the room temperature. Jungle made the world feel alive; Fossil makes it feel buried, haunted, and waiting to be uncovered. The legendary birds give the sky a mythic ceiling, Gengar gives the caves a grin, Dragonite gives the set a soft surprise, and Mysterious Fossil makes the idea of recovery mechanical. It is not just a set of old creatures. It is a lesson in how Pokemon turns absence into play.

claims.text: The local catalog, Pokemon TCG API, and Bulbapedia identify Magneton as Fossil card #11, a Rare Holo Stage 1 Lightning Pokemon evolving from Magnemite and credited to Ken Sugimori.
Bulbapedia and the local Japanese pre-English catalog identify the Japanese source lane as Mystery of the Fossils Magneton, レアコイル / Reakoiru, before the English Fossil release.

The local catalog and Pokemon TCG API record Fossil Magneton #11 with 80 HP, Fighting weakness, two-Colorless retreat, Sonicboom for 20 that ignores Weakness and Resistance, and Selfdestruct for 100 that also deals 20 to each Benched Pokemon and 100 to Magneton itself.

The local catalog, Pokemon TCG API, and Bulbapedia identify a matching Fossil non-holo Magneton as #26, Rare, with the same Ken Sugimori credit, Stage 1 Lightning profile, Sonicboom, Selfdestruct, and 80 HP.

The local Legendary Collection row preserves a later English Magneton branch credited to Ken Sugimori; it should be treated as a later reprint boundary, not evidence that a seller has the Fossil #11 holo.
The Pokemon TCG API models Fossil as set id base3 with releaseDate 1999/10/10 and total 62; Bulbapedia describes Fossil as the English expansion corresponding to Japan's Mystery of the Fossils.
The local catalog, Pokemon TCG API, local Japanese pre-English row, and Bulbapedia credit Fossil Magneton #11/#26 and the Mystery of the Fossils Magneton source lane to Ken Sugimori.

Bulbapedia describes Ken Sugimori as a Japanese video game designer, illustrator, manga artist, co-founder of Game Freak, and central Pokemon franchise art director / character designer; this makes a Sugimori Fossil Magneton a core species-model memory rather than a late decorative reinterpretation.

The local Fossil flavor text says Magneton is formed by several Magnemites linked together and frequently appears when sunspots flare up; Bulbapedia's species page preserves the broader linked-Magnemite, magnetism, and electronics-disruption identity around Magneton.
Local Base Set and Base Set 2 Magneton branches are Keiji Kinebuchi cards with 60 HP, Thunder Wave, and Selfdestruct; Fossil Magneton is a Ken Sugimori 80 HP Sonicboom / Selfdestruct branch.

Local Team Rocket Dark Magneton and Gym Heroes Lt. Surge's Magneton rows are separate character-and-trainer branches with their own artists, attacks, and narrative charge; they should not be folded into Fossil Magneton by name alone.

Bulbapedia's Origin note says Sonic Boom is a move in the Pokemon games that Magneton can learn, while Self-Destruct is a move in the games that Magneton cannot learn; the Fossil card therefore carries both species resonance and early-TCG mechanical exaggeration.

Fossil Magneton matters because it brings a non-organic, assembled, unstable machine life into a set otherwise remembered for bones, birds, ghosts, and recovered ancient bodies: Sonicboom names controlled signal, while Selfdestruct turns linked energy into a risk event.

Because Magneton routes through Fossil #11, Fossil #26, Japanese Mystery of the Fossils, Legendary Collection, Base Set / Base Set 2, Dark Magneton, Lt. Surge's Magneton, Magnemite, and generic species memory, agents must keep row, finish, expansion, artist branch, and trainer/dark variants separate before any trade action.

narrative.human_title: Magneton #11 - sunspots in the fossil bed
narrative.why_it_matters: Fossil Magneton is not ancient in the obvious way. It is not a shell, bone, ghost, or bird. It is three machine lives locked into one magnetic event, and that makes it one of the set's strangest inhabitants: a little storm sitting in the same binder pocket as revived prehistory. Sugimori's credit matters here because it keeps the card close to the franchise's original visual grammar; this is not a later remix of Magneton, it is the species model brought into Fossil's cave air. The attacks make the row even better. Sonicboom is clean signal: damage that slips past Weakness and Resistance. Selfdestruct is the opposite: 100 damage, bench splash, and Magneton destroying itself. Bulbapedia's origin note adds the tiny historical burr that Sonic Boom is a game move Magneton can learn while Self-Destruct is not, so the card sits right at the edge where early TCG design translates species feeling into game drama rather than simply copying the cartridge. For an agent, the romance only helps if the boundaries stay sharp: #11 holo is not #26 non-holo, Japanese Mystery is not automatic English equivalence, Legendary Collection is later, Base/Base 2 are Keiji Kinebuchi 60 HP cards, and Dark or Lt. Surge's Magneton are different branches entirely.

narrative.human_title: The little hinge under the whole set
narrative.why_it_matters: Mysterious Fossil is humble, but it is the hinge. Without it, Fossil is mostly a theme; with it, the theme becomes a rule. Kinebuchi's trainer row tells the agent that the set's deepest idea is not just old Pokemon. It is the act of bringing something buried into play.
